documents.title: Gynecologic oncology surveillance letter
documents.author: gynecologic oncology
documents.body:
Gynecologic Oncology — Surveillance Visit
Date of service: 01/14/2021

Dear Doctor,

Mrs. Kenney returns 6 months after TAH, BSO and staging for a stage IA adult granulosa cell tumor of the left ovary. She feels well. No vaginal bleeding, abdominal pain or bloating.

Exam: abdomen soft, incision well healed, no masses. Pelvic: vaginal cuff intact and smooth, no masses on bimanual or rectovaginal exam.

Serum inhibin B: within normal limits.

No evidence of recurrence. Next visit in 6 months with inhibin B.

Gynecologic Oncology

documents.title: Office Visit — Urinary Infection
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: Two days of cloudy, strong-smelling urine when she caths, with a dull ache over the bladder. No fever, chills or flank pain. Feels this is like her old infections. Last one was before she came to us.

O: afebrile, vitals as charted. Mild suprapubic tenderness, no CVA tenderness. No ptosis or weakness.

UA (cath specimen): leukocyte esterase 2+, nitrite positive, WBC 20-50.

A/P: cystitis in a patient on intermittent catheterization.
- Cephalexin 500 mg BID x 7 days. Chose it over a fluoroquinolone because of her myasthenia.
- Culture sent; will adjust if needed.
- Fresh catheter each time; fluids.

documents.title: Urine culture
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Irene, the culture grew E. coli that is sensitive to the cephalexin you're taking, so finish the full 7 days. Let me know if you aren't clearly better by the weekend.

documents.title: Re: Urine culture
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Thank you. Already much better, urine is clear today.

documents.title: Medicare Annual Wellness Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
MEDICARE ANNUAL WELLNESS VISIT

First in-person wellness visit in two years. Health risk assessment: independent with all daily activities, drives locally, still archiving at the library two mornings a week now that it has reopened. Husband well. No falls. Uses grab bar in shower.

Interval: UTI in March cleared with cephalexin. Gyn onc in January, no recurrence; next in July. Both COVID doses done.

PHQ-2 0. Memory: no concerns; good recall of recent events.

Exam: vitals as charted. No ptosis. Thyroid not enlarged, neck scar healed. Lungs with diminished bases, no wheeze. Heart regular. Abdomen soft, midline scar healed. Knees crepitant, no effusion. No edema.

Prevention: mammogram October, negative. Colonoscopy 2017. No more cervical screening (hysterectomy). Shingrix complete. Pneumococcal: PCV20 at the fall visit. Advance directive: health care proxy copy on file.

Labs: BMP, CBC, lipids.
Neurology video visit next month.

documents.title: Neurology video follow-up
documents.author: neurology
documents.body:
Neurology Clinic — Video Visit
Date of service: 05/12/2021

Dear Colleague,

Yearly review by video for generalized myasthenia gravis after thymectomy and relapsing-remitting MS. Interval history noted: parathyroid adenoma removed February 2020 and a stage IA ovarian granulosa cell tumor removed July 2020; she tolerated both anesthetics without myasthenic weakness.

Myasthenia: no ptosis, diplopia, dysphagia or fatigable limb weakness. On video, no ptosis on sustained upgaze, speech normal through counting to 50, arm abduction sustained.

MS: no relapse. Bladder managed by intermittent catheterization; one UTI this year.

Plan: pyridostigmine 60 mg three times daily, unchanged. In-person visit next year.

Neurology Clinic

documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Doing well. Saw gyn onc in July, she says the exam and blood test were fine; we didn't get a letter. Next visit there in winter.

COPD: unchanged, no flares, walks most days. Theophylline as before.
MG/MS: quiet; neurology video visit in May, no change.
HTN: at goal.
Knees: manageable.

Exam: vitals as charted. No ptosis. Lungs diminished at the bases, no wheeze. Heart regular. No edema.

Plan: PCV20 today (PPSV23 was 2016). Flu and COVID booster already given. Mammogram next month. Wellness visit April.

documents.title: Emergency department physician record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT PHYSICIAN RECORD
Arrival: 07/08/2022 19:15   Departure: 07/09/2022 09:40

Chief complaint: palpitations, nausea, feeling restless.

HPI: 70-year-old woman with myasthenia gravis (generalized; thymectomy 2005), relapsing-remitting MS with neurogenic bladder and moderate COPD. A few hours before arrival she noticed her heart racing, then nausea and an inability to sit still, all getting steadily worse. Takes theophylline for COPD long term. Was seen here 2 days ago for a urinary infection and started on ciprofloxacin; urine culture from that visit is growing Proteus.

Medications per patient: pyridostigmine 60 mg TID, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily, acetaminophen PRN, vitamin D3, calcium carbonate, ciprofloxacin 500 mg BID (started 07/06). Theophylline per narrative above.
Allergies: NKDA.
Social: former smoker, occasional wine.

Triage vitals: BP 150/90, HR 110, RR 20, T 37.0 C.
Exam: anxious and restless, conversant. Mild expiratory wheezing both sides. Heart tachycardic, regular. Abdomen soft. No focal neurologic deficit; no ptosis.

Results: serum theophylline 25 mcg/mL (therapeutic 5-15). Creatinine 1.2, BUN 18. Liver tests normal. ECG sinus tachycardia, no other abnormality.

MDM: theophylline toxicity, most likely from reduced clearance after starting ciprofloxacin. Theophylline held. IV fluids. Cardiac monitoring overnight: sinus tachycardia only, rate settled into the 80s by morning; nausea and restlessness resolved. Repeat level overnight falling.

Diagnoses: theophylline toxicity; urinary tract infection, Proteus.
Disposition: home 07/09. HOLD theophylline until reviewed by PCP. Continue ciprofloxacin to complete 7 days. Follow up with PCP within 1 week; return for chest pain, fainting, vomiting or any new weakness.

Emergency Medicine

documents.title: Discharge summary — medical ICU
documents.author: critical care
documents.body:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admitted: 07/10/2022 (medical ICU)   Discharged: 07/19/2022

Principal diagnosis: myasthenic crisis.
Other diagnoses: urinary tract infection, Proteus (diagnosed in our ED 07/06); theophylline toxicity (ED 07/08), resolved; COPD; hypertension; relapsing-remitting MS with neurogenic bladder; history of ovarian granulosa cell tumor and of parathyroid adenoma, both resected.

History: 70-year-old woman with generalized myasthenia gravis after thymectomy. On 07/06 she came to our ED with fever, chills, lower abdominal pain and cloudy, foul-smelling urine, with harder voiding despite her usual intermittent catheterization; she was tender over the bladder, urinalysis was alkaline with many white cells and crystals, an abdominal film showed no radiopaque stones, and she was sent home on ciprofloxacin. Culture grew Proteus. On 07/08 she returned with theophylline toxicity (level 25), theophylline was held and she went home the next morning. She came back 07/10 with two days of worsening breathlessness and weakness that began after the antibiotic was started.

On arrival: working to breathe with accessory muscles, speaking in short phrases. T 37.8 C, BP 145/90, HR 88, RR 26, SpO2 92% on room air. Bilateral ptosis and diplopia. Breath sounds diminished on both sides with a prolonged expiratory phase. Cough weak. Unable to raise her head from the pillow. ABG: pH 7.32, PaCO2 50, PaO2 70, HCO3 24.

Hospital course:
- Myasthenic crisis, likely provoked by ciprofloxacin in the setting of infection. Admitted to the ICU. BiPAP for 3 days; intubation was not needed. IVIG 0.4 g/kg daily for 5 days. Pyridostigmine held while on BiPAP and restarted on hospital day 4 at 60 mg three times daily. Neurology followed daily. Neck and limb strength improved steadily; ptosis and diplopia resolved by day 6. Transferred to the floor day 5, worked with PT, walking the hall independently at discharge.
- UTI: ciprofloxacin stopped on admission; ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily to complete 7 days of treatment. Afebrile from day 2.
- Theophylline toxicity: theophylline kept on hold for the whole stay; no arrhythmia.
- Creatinine returned to her baseline.

Discharge medications: pyridostigmine 60 mg three times daily; hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily; acetaminophen 500 mg as needed; vitamin D3 2000 units daily; calcium carbonate 500 mg twice daily.
HELD: theophylline, pending review by her primary care physician.

Medications to avoid in myasthenia: fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, macrolides, IV magnesium, and others per neurology handout given to the patient.

Follow-up: primary care within 1 week; neurology 08/15/2022.

Critical Care Medicine

documents.title: Call from husband — in ICU
documents.author: RN
documents.body:
Husband called to let us know she was admitted to the ICU at the regional hospital yesterday with a myasthenia flare; she is on a breathing mask, not a ventilator. He says she was in the ER twice last week, first for a bladder infection, then for a racing heart from her theophylline. We have no records of either ER visit. Pt has given verbal permission in the past to speak with husband (HCP on file).

Requested ED records and will ask for discharge summary. PCP aware. Husband will call when discharge is planned.

documents.title: Transitional care call
documents.author: RN
documents.body:
Post-discharge call, pt discharged 7/19. Spoke with pt and husband. Breathing comfortable, voice strong, eyelids normal, walking around the house and short distances outside. Eating well, catheterizing without problems, urine clear, no fever.

Meds reviewed from discharge paperwork: pyridostigmine 60 TID, HCTZ, acetaminophen PRN, vitamin D, calcium. Theophylline on hold per hospital. Cipro stopped in hospital. She has the hospital's list of medicines to avoid.

PCP visit Friday 7/22. Told to call 911 for any trouble breathing or swallowing.

medications.drug_text: theophylline 200 MG Extended Release Oral Tablet
medications.sig: Take 1 tablet by mouth twice daily

documents.title: Hospital Follow-up Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Transitional care visit; discharged 7/19 after a 9-day stay. Husband with her. She brought the discharge paperwork; the formal summary hasn't arrived and we still have no note from the 7/6 ER visit. The 7/8 ER record came by fax last week.

Sequence as she and the paperwork tell it: 7/6 ER for a Proteus bladder infection, given ciprofloxacin. 7/8 ER with a racing heart, nausea and restlessness, theophylline level 25, theophylline stopped, cipro continued. 7/10 admitted to the ICU with myasthenic crisis: ptosis, double vision, weak neck and cough, CO2 retention. BiPAP 3 days, IVIG 5 days, no intubation. Cipro changed to ceftriaxone.

Today: feels about 80% of normal and better each day. No double vision, no droopy lids, swallowing normal. Breathing back to her usual. Tired after the walk to the mailbox. Urine clear, no fever.

Exam: vitals as charted. Lids open fully, no ptosis on sustained upgaze. Speech clear. Neck flexion strong, arms and legs full strength. Lungs diminished at the bases, no wheeze. Heart regular.

A/P
1. Myasthenic crisis, recovering. Pyridostigmine 60 TID. Neurology 8/15. Reviewed the hospital's list of drugs to avoid; copy scanned.
2. Theophylline toxicity, resolved; the cause (ciprofloxacin) is gone. She has been on theophylline for years with levels 11-12. Restart 200 mg BID today, level in 1 week.
3. Proteus UTI, treated. Resolved.
4. HTN: fine on HCTZ.

Follow up after neurology, about 2 months.

documents.title: Discharge summary received and reviewed
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: ICU discharge summary from the regional hospital received today and reviewed; matches what the patient brought on 7/22. Medication list reconciled: theophylline was held at discharge, restarted here 7/22. ED record from 7/6 still not received; second request sent.

documents.title: Theophylline level
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Irene, theophylline level 10.6 on the usual dose, in range. Kidney function is back to your normal. Stay on 200 mg twice a day. Please remind anyone who prescribes you an antibiotic about the myasthenia list.

documents.title: Neurology follow-up after myasthenic crisis
documents.author: neurology
documents.body:
Neurology Clinic — Follow-up
Date of service: 08/15/2022

Dear Colleague,

I saw Mrs. Kenney a month after her ICU admission for myasthenic crisis, which followed a course of ciprofloxacin for a Proteus urinary infection. She was treated with IVIG and BiPAP and did not require intubation.

She now feels back to her usual self. No ptosis, diplopia, dysphagia or dyspnea beyond her COPD baseline.

Exam: no ptosis after one minute of upgaze; extraocular movements full; facial and bulbar strength normal; neck flexion and limb strength full without fatigability. MS exam unchanged.

Assessment: generalized myasthenia gravis, recovered from a medication-provoked crisis.

Plan: pyridostigmine 60 mg three times daily, unchanged. Avoid fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, macrolides and magnesium; she has our written list. Return in 12 months, or sooner with any bulbar or respiratory symptoms.

Neurology Clinic

documents.title: Office Visit — Follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Two months out from the crisis. Back to full activity: dog walks, two mornings at the archive. Neurology 8/15 agreed she has recovered; no medication change.

Breathing at her baseline on theophylline; level 10.6 in July. No palpitations or nausea.

The 7/6 ER note never came despite two requests; the discharge summary covers it.

Exam: vitals as charted. No ptosis. Lungs diminished, no wheeze. Heart regular. Strength full.

A/P: myasthenic crisis resolved; MG back to baseline. COPD, HTN stable. Flu shot and new COVID booster next month. Gyn onc visit in winter.
